ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure, the left side is an upward current source I_s, in parallel with resistor R_s between the upper and lower two nodes; the top is connected through switch S to the right-side branch. The right-side branch is composed of resistor R and inductor L in series, and current i(t) is marked in the clockwise direction. The switch is shown in the figure as originally open, and the problem states that it closes at t=0. Reasoning: After the switch closes, the network of the left-side current source in parallel with R_s can be equivalent to a Thevenin source, whose open-circuit voltage is V_th = I_s R_s. Since the switch is open when t<0, the right-side R-L branch is not excited by the source, so the initial inductor current is 0; the inductor current cannot change abruptly, therefore i(0+) = 0. Thus at t=0+, the voltage drop across resistor R is R i(0+) = 0, and the Thevenin voltage is all applied to inductor L. From v_L = L di/dt, obtain L(di/dt)(0+) = I_s R_s, so (di/dt)(0+) = R_s I_s / L.

raw_record.question_text: In the following circuit, the switch \(S\) is closed at \(t=0\). What is \(\frac{di}{dt}(0^+)\)?

method.method_draft: First identify from the image that the right branch is a series R-L branch connected to the left source network only when S closes. Replace the left current-source-plus-R_s network by its Thevenin equivalent, V_th=I_s R_s. Since the switch was open before t=0, the inductor current is initially zero and remains zero at 0^+, so there is no instantaneous voltage drop across R. Therefore the entire Thevenin voltage appears across L at 0^+, giving L(di/dt)(0^+)=R_s I_s, hence (di/dt)(0^+)=R_s I_s/L.
